title: Levers
prompt: A clearly labelled teaching adaptation of the Levers principle using a rigid bench lever with repositionable fulcrum, load and effort attachment points. Lift applies effort to raise the load. Move fulcrum compares effort and travel at unchanged load. Change class repositions the actual fulcrum, effort and load into the three supported orders. Show force arrows, perpendicular moment arms and travel distances. At slow equilibrium compare effort times moment arm with load times moment arm. Do not add hidden drives to explain leverage.
blurb: An adjustable teaching adaptation compares the force and travel of three lever classes.

identity.note: Levers chapter. Page 18 explains effort, load and arm lengths. Pages 19, 20 and 21 distinguish first-, second- and third-class geometry and the force versus travel tradeoff.

adaptationDecision.reason: Explicit principle adaptation. It compares classes and arm lengths. The named tool rows are applications, rather than duplicates of this adjustable comparison rig.

prompt.note: Faithful teaching adaptation if real pivot, load and effort positions change. Moving labels alone cannot change lever class. The adjustable bench rig is an adaptation, not a pictured book machine.

adaptation.identity: Explicit principle teaching adaptation. The adjustable bench rig is not a pictured book machine.
adaptation.fixtures: Drilled rigid beam, rail-clamped two-cheek fulcrum with transverse pin and sleeve, load hanger, effort cross pin and grip. Generic representative geometry.
adaptation.actions: Lift and Lower model slow external effort on the grip. Move fulcrum and Change class require a lowered lever and represent an operator supporting the unchanged load and refitting the apparatus. No hidden drives.
adaptation.physics: Ideal massless rigid beam, frictionless fixed pivot, vertical external effort and unchanged 100 N load. Neglects fixture mass and inertia. E = 100 * abs(load-pivot)/abs(effort-pivot). Perpendicular arms are horizontal projections. Travel values are vertical displacements through a 12 degree stroke.
adaptation.overlays: Force arrows, right-angle moment-arm brackets and travel traces are overlays. They do not count as anatomy. Force arrow lengths are schematic.
